taskTitle: Twelve HTTP status codes, by the book

checks.detail: 3 proposers ran in parallel, one per lens
4 phases had the tools designed for them

finalText:
All twelve codes are taken from RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics, STD 97), https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html. Each entry comes from the code's own subsection of Section 15, not the overview list or table of contents.

- Cacheability rule: Section 15.1 says: "Responses with status codes that are defined as heuristically cacheable (e.g., 200, 203, 204, 206, 300, 301, 308, 404, 405, 410, 414, and 501 in this specification) can be reused by a cache with heuristic expiration". It adds that all other status codes are not heuristically cacheable.
- Cacheable among the twelve: 203, 206, 308, 405, 410, 414 and 501 are heuristically cacheable. 303, 307, 413, 421 and 422 are not.
- Per-section check: the sections for 203, 308, 410, 414 and 501 state it explicitly. The 405 section states it in its cacheability sentence, which is not among the quotes.
- Meaning of false: responses with explicit freshness information can still be cached. "False" only means the code is not heuristically cacheable by default.
- Reason phrases: RFC 9110 renamed 413 to "Content Too Large" (it was "Payload Too Large" in RFC 7231) and 422 to "Unprocessable Content".
- Quotes: the 422 quote may wrap across a line on the page, so it may need whitespace normalisation when checked.
- Supersession: I did not check whether any newer RFC replaces RFC 9110. I am treating it as the current specification.
